text: Welcome to Machine Learning Fundamentals, step five of the Data Scientist path. You already know Python, pandas, statistics and how to explore data. Now we learn how a machine can learn from it, starting with the big question: what is machine learning, really?

In traditional programming, you write the rules. Rules plus data give you answers. Machine learning flips that. You give the computer data together with the answers, and it works out the rules itself. Those learned rules are called a model, and the whole point is to reuse the model on new data, where the answer isn't known yet.

Here is the difference in code, using house prices. At the top, a hand-written function with thresholds somebody guessed. Below it, a linear regression model that calls fit on square footage and known prices. Same job, but the second version finds its own numbers from sixty examples. All of these figures are illustrative.

Ask both about an eighteen hundred square foot house. The rule says three hundred twenty thousand. The learned model says about two hundred sixty-one thousand, and we can inspect what it learned: roughly one hundred nineteen dollars per extra square foot, on top of a base near forty-six thousand. Neither is magic. The model is just a pattern extracted from examples.

This chart is the output of the code above. The dots are the examples, and the red line is the learned pattern. Learning here means adjusting numbers until the line fits the examples well. Every algorithm in this course is a more powerful version of that same idea.

One last thing to remember. The real test isn't how well a model fits the data it has already seen. It's how it performs on data it hasn't. That idea runs through everything ahead. Up next, lesson two: supervised versus unsupervised learning.
